_metadata.correction: owner's corrected rubric relayed 2026-10-17: no minimum hint count, no board competition, generic allowed when natural to both words, compounds judged as compounds
_metadata.independence: I read only u02-pilot-blind-input.json and no other file, search result, or prior scoring; all judgements are from my own general knowledge.
_metadata.changes_from_v1: Compound rule upgraded CROSS (bridge/fire, crossfire), STONE (bridge/key, keystone), BACK (diamond/snake, diamondback) and BRAND (fire/iron, firebrand) from BORDERLINE to PASS and lifted BURN's heart score to 2 via heartburn; no hint was ever lowered for generic-ness or board competition, so nothing else moved.

hints.reason: A forge is a fire used to heat and work iron; both sides are immediate.
Fire is hot, and 'hot iron' / 'strike while the iron is hot' is a standard phrase; generic but natural to both.
A blacksmith works iron (direct) at a fire (one step via the forge); same idea as FORGE.
Branding iron is direct; fire comes through the familiar compound firebrand and the older sense of a burning stick.

pairs.pair_note: Strong pair; FORGE is the natural answer, HOT a safe backup, SMITH duplicates FORGE, and BRAND is the weakest PASS.

hints.reason: A match starts a fire and you 'light a match'; both senses immediate.
Candlelight is direct; candle to fire goes through the flame, one small step.
A torch is burning fire carried for light; torchlight is a common word.
A spark ignites fire and is itself a tiny flash of light.

pairs.pair_note: Very easy pair; every hint works, with CANDLE and TORCH resting on the same burning-light-source idea.

hints.reason: You cast a shadow and cast light on something; both collocations are everyday.
Dark is the direct opposite of light and the substance of a shadow; generic but natural to both.
Shadow puppet is direct; the lamp behind the puppet is a second step most players will not make unprompted.
Sunlight is immediate; sun to shadow requires thinking about what the sun produces behind an object.

pairs.pair_note: CAST is the elegant answer and DARK the blunt one; PUPPET and SUN lean on the shadow or light side respectively.

hints.reason: Bank vault is direct; diamonds being kept in a vault is plausible but not a phrase anyone reaches for.
Bank heist and diamond heist are both stock movie phrases.
A safe belongs to a bank; a diamond in a safe is only an inferred location.

pairs.pair_note: HEIST carries the pair alone; VAULT and SAFE are the same bank-side idea with diamond as an afterthought.

hints.reason: 'Burn your bridges' is a universal idiom and fire burns.
Cross a bridge is direct and crossfire is a familiar compound; judged as compounds both sides are reached.
London Bridge is famous; the Great Fire of London is history many US adults will not recall in time.

pairs.pair_note: BURN is the obvious hint and CROSS a fair compound play; LONDON is bridge-first with fire attached by a history lesson.

hints.reason: A song has a bridge section and is written in a key; both are common musical terms.
Key as island (Florida Keys) and a bridge to an island are each one stretch; neither side is direct.
Stone bridge is a natural phrase and keystone a familiar compound; a bonus is that the keystone is itself part of an arch bridge.

pairs.pair_note: SONG is a clean double meaning and STONE a fair compound play; ISLAND needs the player to assemble the link.

hints.reason: The Statue of Liberty's spiked crown is iconic; light comes only through her torch and that is a second step.
A halo is a ring of light; calling it a crown is a shape analogy, not a phrase a stranger reaches for.
The sun's corona is a crown of light, but corona meaning crown is Latin most US players know only via beer or the virus.

pairs.pair_note: No clean hint: all three reach one side strongly and the other only by a figurative or etymological step.

hints.reason: Diamond is a crystal and salt forms crystals; both direct.
Rock salt is a product name and a diamond is a 'rock' in everyday slang.
Diamond mine and salt mine are both familiar phrases.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent pair; all three hints are direct on both sides.

hints.reason: Fire burns directly; heartburn is an everyday compound, judged as such.
Passion is fiery and heartfelt; a mood hint, but both metaphors are standard.
A warm fire and a warm heart are both everyday phrases.

pairs.pair_note: Solid pair; all three hints reach both words without explanation.

hints.reason: Wildfire and wild horse are both immediate.
Firebrand gets partway to fire, but branding is associated with cattle far more than horses; both sides need a step.
Trojan Horse is famous; fire only via the burning of Troy, which must be explained.

pairs.pair_note: WILD is the only hint that reaches both sides without a story; TROJAN is horse-only in practice.

hints.reason: The Headless Horseman is a ghost on a horse; one reference reaches both sides at once.
Ghosts are pale; the pale horse of Revelation is a reference many players will not make.
A rider rides a horse, and Ghost Rider (comics, film, Johnny Cash song) is a widely known phrase.

pairs.pair_note: Two good hints; HEADLESS is the single-reference ideal, RIDER is a strong plain-sense plus pop-culture pair.

hints.reason: Lights flicker directly; flickering lights as a haunting sign is a trope the player must supply.
An orb of light is direct; 'ghost orbs' are a ghost-hunting term unknown to most.
Shining light is direct; The Shining is a famous ghost story but the title alone does not say ghost.

pairs.pair_note: Every hint is light-first with ghost reached only through a haunting trope or a film title.

hints.reason: The heart pumps blood and blood contains iron; both facts are common knowledge.
The heart is a pump and 'pump iron' means lifting weights.
Heart as the core of something and Earth's iron core are each a step away.
Cold heart is direct; 'cold iron' is a literary phrase few would reach for.

pairs.pair_note: PUMP and BLOOD are both excellent; CORE and COLD are weaker and lean on one side.

hints.reason: Bees make honey; bees being active in spring is seasonal background, not a link.
Spring blossom is direct; honey from blossoms (orange blossom honey) is a secondary association.
Pollen season is spring; bees gathering pollen to make honey is how most people picture honey-making.

pairs.pair_note: A soft pair; POLLEN is the one hint that sits between both words, while BEE and BLOSSOM each face one of them.

hints.reason: Horseshoe is an immediate compound; there is no 'shoe + iron' compound, so iron is only reached by recalling the material.
A blacksmith works iron and the classic image is of him shoeing a horse.
Both sides depend on knowing the nickname 'iron horse' for a locomotive, and TRAIN itself is not part of that compound.

pairs.pair_note: SMITH is the one defensible hint; SHOE is horse-only and TRAIN needs the 'iron horse' nickname.

hints.reason: Derby is a horse race; the Kentucky Derby's 'Run for the Roses' is a detail only fans know.
War horse is a stock phrase and the War(s) of the Roses is well known from history and the film title.
Horse blanket is fine, but the Derby's 'blanket of roses' is trivia a stranger will not reach.

pairs.pair_note: WAR works; DERBY and BLANKET both lean on the same obscure Kentucky Derby rose tradition.

hints.reason: Iron is heavy and heavy is the opposite of light.
Light glows; hot iron glowing is true but needs the player to picture a forge.
Cast iron and cast light are both standard collocations.

pairs.pair_note: CAST is the elegant double meaning and HEAVY the sturdy antonym; GLOW is light-only.

hints.reason: Roses bloom and spring is the season of bloom.
Rosebud is a word and buds appear in spring.
Rose garden is direct; spring gardening is a seasonal association rather than a phrase, so the spring side is the weak one, not the generic-ness.

pairs.pair_note: BLOOM and BUD are both strong but are the same flowering idea; GARDEN leans toward rose.

hints.reason: Bank vault is direct; a key for the vault is an inferred detail.
Bank deposit is direct; 'key deposit' is a real but unfamiliar phrase and the safe-deposit-box key is a thin reach.
Lock and key is direct; lock to bank goes through vault or lockbox.

pairs.pair_note: All three hints sit on the security idea but each reaches only one word cleanly; the pair lacks a real double meaning.

hints.reason: Blood bank is a common phrase and the heart pumps blood.
Robbers steal from banks and someone 'steals your heart'.
Trust companies and 'trust your heart' are each one step removed.

pairs.pair_note: Two strong hints from different angles; TRUST is abstract on both sides.

hints.reason: Horse stable is direct; a 'stable bank' is an adjective use a player may not connect.
A bank charge is direct; a cavalry charge reaches horse only by a step.
Betting on horses is direct; bank as the house or bankroll in gambling is a stretch.

pairs.pair_note: Nothing clean here; each hint is a real pun on one side and a strained one on the other.

hints.reason: Iron bar is direct; gold bars in a bank is an inferred image and there is no 'bank bar' phrase.
Piggy bank is a familiar near-compound, but 'pig iron' is a term most non-specialists have at best heard of and could not place.
Bank safe is direct; iron as the material of a safe is a secondary thought.

pairs.pair_note: PIG is clever and the closest to passing, but pig iron is half-obscure; BAR and SAFE each reach only one word with confidence.

hints.reason: A dentist fits both bridges and crowns; the dental sense is familiar to most US adults.
A tooth gets a crown or is replaced by a bridge; same dental idea as DENTIST.
London Bridge is direct; the Crown Jewels or the British Crown is a looser association.
Arch bridge is direct, but the 'crown' of an arch is an architecture term nobody outside the trade uses.

pairs.pair_note: The dental double meaning carries the pair, though both PASS hints are the same idea; ARCH does not reach crown.

hints.reason: Bridge is a card game and hearts is a card suit and game.
Cross a bridge and 'cross my heart' are both everyday phrases.
Bridge the gap is direct; there is no natural route from gap to heart.

pairs.pair_note: Two good hints of different flavors; GAP is bridge-only.

hints.reason: Pooh and honey are inseparable, but the Poohsticks bridge is a detail almost no US adult will summon.
Rainbow Bridge at Niagara and Niagara as honeymoon capital are both trivia; neither side is reachable cold.
Dental bridge is direct; honey is reached only via 'sweet tooth', which is not a compound with honey.
Honey is golden; 'golden bridge' is not a phrase, so bridge is reached only by completing the Golden Gate name.

pairs.pair_note: A hard pair with no fair hint; GOLDEN is the best of a weak set and still a colour clue plus a landmark name.

hints.reason: Hamlet is a prince fighting over a stolen crown and is driven by his father's ghost; both are the play's core.
King to crown is immediate; king to ghost needs Hamlet's ghost king or a Stephen King detour.
Haunted castle is a stock image and a castle is where crowned royalty live.

pairs.pair_note: HAMLET is the ideal single-reference hint for those who know the play; CASTLE is the plain-sense fallback.

hints.reason: A queen wears a crown and the Queen of Hearts is a famous card and character.
A king wears a crown and the King of Hearts is a playing card.
Hearts is a suit; crown only via the pictures on face cards.

pairs.pair_note: QUEEN is the stronger of two near-identical royal-card hints; CARD is heart-first.

hints.reason: Queen to crown is immediate; honey needs queen bee and then the hive, two steps.
Royal to crown is direct; royal jelly is a bee product, not honey, and is obscure anyway.
Mead is honey wine for those who know it, but nothing about mead points to a crown.

pairs.pair_note: No fair hint; QUEEN is the only one that even gestures at both words.

hints.reason: Cursed diamonds (Hope Diamond) and curses bringing ghosts are each a stretch.
A haunted tower is a loose image and tower to diamond requires knowing the Crown Jewels sit in the Tower of London.
Ghosts vanish; a diamond vanishing is only a heist plot, not a property of diamonds.

pairs.pair_note: An unnatural pairing; CURSE is the only hint with a foothold on both words and it is weak.

hints.reason: A diamond's cut is its key quality and cut roses are what florists sell.
Diamond rings and roses are the two standard tokens of love.
Pink roses are everywhere; pink diamonds exist but are a specialist thought.

pairs.pair_note: CUT is a satisfying double meaning and LOVE a natural generic; PINK is a colour hint that favors rose.

hints.reason: Judged as a compound, diamondback is a familiar word and it names a rattlesnake, so one compound reaches both words; snake is one step behind diamond.
Diamond pattern is a stock phrase; snakeskin pattern is a secondary association, so the snake side is the weak one.
Snake scales are direct; diamond to scale requires the Mohs hardness or carat scale.

pairs.pair_note: The pair is really the word 'diamondback', and BACK is the hint that invokes it; PATTERN and SCALE each favor one side.

hints.reason: Locked points straight to key but nothing about it points to ghost.
Skeleton key is a common term and skeletons sit beside ghosts in every spooky lineup.
House key is direct; ghost arrives only by adding 'haunted', since 'ghost house' is not the phrase.

pairs.pair_note: SKELETON is an excellent hint; the other two are key-first.

hints.reason: Bees make honey; a bee visiting a rose is incidental.
Honey is made from nectar and nectar is what a flower like a rose holds; the flower link is the natural next thought.
Honey is sweet; a rose smelling sweet is poetic rather than immediate, so the rose side is the weak one.

pairs.pair_note: A gentle pair where NECTAR bridges both words; BEE and SWEET are honey-first.

hints.reason: Honey is sweet and 'sweet and salty' is such a fixed pairing that salt is reachable as the contrast.
Salt lick is a set phrase; licking honey is just something one might do.
Salt cures meat; honey-cured or honey as a folk remedy is a secondary thought.

pairs.pair_note: SWEET works through contrast; LICK and CURE are salt-first with honey tacked on.

hints.reason: You press a key, and pressing a rose in a book is a familiar keepsake practice.
A map has a key (legend) and a compass rose; both are standard map vocabulary.
Rose garden is direct, but nothing leads from garden to key short of The Secret Garden's locked door.

pairs.pair_note: MAP is a neat double meaning and PRESS a good plain-sense hint; GARDEN is rose-only.

hints.reason: You wind a clock or toy with a key, which tightens its spring; spring breezes give a second route.
Lock and key is immediate; a spring-loaded lock is mechanical detail.
A wind-up clock has a key and a mainspring, but neither is the first thing a player thinks of for clock.

pairs.pair_note: WIND is the one hint that reaches both words from a single wind-up image; CLOCK is the same idea one step further away.
